entities.name: Antipater of Bostra
entities.label: Person
entities.summary:
Antipater of Bostra, a Greek prelate serving as Metropolitan bishop of Bostra in the Roman province of Arabia, emerged as one of the most fervent and influential critics of Origen in the mid-5th century CE. Flourishing around 450 CE, Antipater's theological contributions were primarily polemical, aimed at refuting the complex and often controversial doctrines of the 3rd-century Alexandrian theologian Origen. His work, particularly 'Antirrheticus' (Against Origen), positioned him as a staunch defender of Chalcedonian orthodoxy during a period of intense Christological and theological debate within the Eastern Roman Empire, thereby shaping the intellectual landscape of early Byzantine Christianity.

Antipater's 'Antirrheticus' systematically attacked Origen's doctrines, particularly those concerning the pre-existence of souls, the transmigration of souls, the apocatastasis (universal salvation), and the subordination of the Son to the Father. Drawing heavily on earlier anti-Origenist arguments, Antipater meticulously compiled a florilegium of Patristic citations to demonstrate Origen's alleged heterodoxy and his deviation from accepted Christian tradition. Although much of 'Antirrheticus' survives only in fragments and through later citations, its impact was significant in solidifying the anti-Origenist consensus that characterized much of the 5th and 6th centuries, contributing to the eventual condemnation of Origen's teachings at the Second Council of Constantinople in 553 CE.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: Antipater of Bostra's rigorous anti-Origenist polemics played a crucial role in shaping orthodox Christian theology in the 5th century, influencing the eventual condemnation of Origen's doctrines and reinforcing Chalcedonian principles for centuries to come.
